channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today’s ranked reading list puts two relevance-4 papers first: 2611.27140, on FPGA-in-loop drift tracking and charge-jump recovery for autonomously retuning spin-qubit operating points, and 2611.27927, on calibration-aware, transpilation-predicted multi-vendor QPU scheduling that could transfer to an HPC queue managing a small noisy spin-qubit device. The two relevance-3 skims follow: 2611.27896 offers an eighth-order Trotter-Suzuki circuit-synthesis plugin and gate-depth comparisons, while 2611.26884 proposes Trotter-step ordering to reduce circuit depth and Trotter error; both are indirectly useful for the software and application-benchmark stack but lack spin-qubit, calibration, or HPC-integration results. No pay dirt today — 1 to read · 1 to skim.

item.title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
item.description:
Read new method — Training-free topology-divergence estimate matches transpile-all device selection at about 25× lower latency, ranking measured success on IBM hardware at Spearman ρ=0.95 and reducing SLA violations from 42–74 jobs down to a few out of 102.

Grade 0.533 · 4.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Accelerating HPC With Quantum Computing: It Is a Software Challenge Too” · Ana Paula Appel

Figure

SLA violations (left) and false rejections (right) versus requested success probability τ for 102 jobs replayed on three IBM Heron devices. Filtering with the topology-divergence estimate keeps violations near zero, whereas raw-fidelity and random placement miss τ for 42 to 83 jobs.

Asks

Can a cluster scheduler automatically select the optimal QPU backend for a given quantum circuit to meet a target fidelity floor without running full transpilation on every candidate device?

Before

Selecting candidate QPUs by highest average device fidelity or via level-1 transpilation for every candidate device; picking by average fidelity produced 42–74 SLA violations out of 102 jobs.

But

Fails across vendors when published calibration figures overstate hardware fidelity (e.g., Rigetti Cepheus by 0.47, AQT IBEX Q1 by 0.25). Device-mean rates cannot differentiate near-identical devices or capture broad output distributions (such as QAOA and VQE). Tested on 6 devices across 4 vendors without neutral-atom targets.

Tools

topology-divergence estimate with VF2 subgraph embedding · two-stage schedule-reserve-transpile-bind protocol · Kubernetes and Slurm scheduling frameworks · Qiskit and tket compilers

Code. https://github.com/anapaulaappel/QPUScheduler

Abstract

Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.

arxave:action.title: Prototype estimator on spin-qubit calibration data

item.arxave:action: Use the 16-qubit spin QPU's connectivity and published 1Q/2Q fidelities to predict post-transpilation success for benchmark circuits, then compare against exact transpile-and-check to see whether the millisecond filter holds for spin-qubit error rates and routing overhead.

arxave:action.title: Can the scheduler query in-session spin-qubit calibration?

item.arxave:action: Ask whether the spin-qubit control stack exposes calibration state and fidelities through an API, and whether a critical job can request a fresh calibration before binding, since the paper shows published telemetry can be stale or misleading.

arxave:action.title: Validate published fidelities before cross-device scheduling

item.arxave:action: The paper fails when published figures overstate a device; for the spin QPU, require periodic benchmark-backed calibration data rather than vendor averages before using the scheduler's hard success-probability filter.

item.title: Scheduling the quantum implementation of the Trotter decomposition for Hamiltonian simulation
item.description:
Skim new method — Cyclic-2 scheduling combining simultaneous diagonalization with traveling-salesman cell CNOT optimization achieves second-order O(t3/r2) Trotter error scaling while preserving first-order sub-unitary count Lr. For a dihydrogen molecular Hamiltonian, it reaches target precision at circuit depth ~200 where prior strategies require depth >1000.

Grade 0.503 · 3.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…” · Augustin Ho (Graduate School of Science and Technology, Keio University, École des Mines de Saint-Étienne), Naoki Yamamoto (Graduate School of Science and Technology, Keio University, Quantum Computing Center, Keio University)

Figure

Error versus circuit depth and Trotter step r for dihydrogen simulation (t=3). Shows cyclic-2 surpassing DepleteGroups for r>3 and matching precision at circuit depth ~200 that requires depth >1000 for static baselines.

Asks

How can the execution order of sub-Hamiltonians in Trotter decomposition be scheduled to simultaneously reduce both algorithmic error and circuit depth without increasing sub-unitary count?

Before

Simultaneous diagonalization, MaxCommuteTSP, and molecular-specific DepleteGroups (all static first-order orderings requiring depth >1000 for the precision cyclic-2 hits at depth ~200 on dihydrogen).

But

Classical simulations only; tested on systems up to n=8 qubits; fourth-order cyclic-10 shows no benefit over cyclic-2 for r≤20 Trotter steps; small circuit depth disadvantage observed for 8-qubit Heisenberg model versus standard simultaneous diagonalization.

Tools

Cyclic-2 alternating forward-backward Trotter scheduling · Simultaneous diagonalization via graph coloring · Cell CNOT optimization via Traveling Salesman Problem heuristics · OpenFermion simulation package

Abstract

For the quantum computational task for Hamiltonian simulation, the arrangement in which sub-Hamiltonians appear in the Trotter decomposition may have a large influence on the precision, under a given circuit complexity. In this paper, we design several scheduling strategies by combining two methods; that is, the existing simultaneous diagonalization scheme leveraged in order to guarantee the performance in a relatively short circuit depth, with a method inspired from a Trotter-Suzuki decomposition of the second or the fourth order for a better accuracy. By conducting numerical simulations on various Hamiltonian instances, we confirm a systematic advantage over previous methods. Thus, our proposal may eliminate the need of dealing with several Hamiltonian-dependent scheduling strategies.
